options.misconception: Used a factor of one hundred rather than one thousand
Reported joules instead of converting to kilojoules
Divided mass by latent heat instead of multiplying
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: During a phase change the temperature stays constant while energy goes into rearranging the structure, so Q equals mass times specific latent heat. Here 147 g times 240 J per g gives 35280 J, or 35.28 kJ after dividing by one thousand.
questions.hint: Q = m L, then convert joules to kilojoules.

questions.stem: Trial 805935314: a 1.4 mol quantity of nitrogen with molar heat capacity 75 J per mol K is heated by 39 K; find the heat supplied in kJ.

options.misconception: Used moles times temperature without the heat capacity
Dropped the number of moles from the calculation
Correct application of the principle
Left the answer in joules instead of kilojoules

questions.explanation: When heat capacity is given per mole, the heat required is Q equals n times Cm times delta T. Multiplying 1.4 mol by 75 J per mol K by 39 K and dividing by one thousand yields 4.09 kJ.

options.misconception: Omitted the metal cooling range from the denominator
Swapped the metal and water temperature changes
Ignored the mass of water in the balance
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: Energy conservation gives heat lost by metal equals heat gained by water, so mm cm (Tim minus Tf) equals mw cw (Tf minus Tiw). Solving for cm with water at 4.184 J per g K gives 3.220 J per g K; the two temperature differences must be kept in their correct positions.

questions.stem: Trial 347731433: an ideal gas of xenon with 2.5 mol expands isothermally at 317 K from 1.4 L to 4.6 L; how much heat must be supplied, in kJ?

options.misconception: Omitted the logarithm from the work expression
Halved the temperature in the nRT factor
Correct application of the principle
Altered the volume ratio by adding one to it

questions.explanation: For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy does not change, so by the first law the heat supplied equals the work done by the gas, nRT ln(Vf over Vi). With the given volumes and temperature this is 7.87 kJ; heat must flow in to balance the expansion work.
questions.hint: At constant T for an ideal gas, Q = W = nRT ln(Vf/Vi).

questions.stem: Trial 893090283: starting at 444 K, an ideal gas of krypton with gamma 1.4 expands adiabatically from 2.3 L to 5.8 L; find the final temperature.

options.misconception: Correct application of the principle
Inverted the initial-to-final volume ratio
Used gamma rather than gamma minus one as the exponent
Assumed temperature scales linearly with volume

questions.explanation: For a reversible adiabatic ideal-gas process T V raised to gamma minus one is constant, so Tf equals Ti times (Vi over Vf) to the power gamma minus one. With gamma 1.4 the exponent is 0.4, giving a final temperature of 307.8 K; expansion cools the gas because it does work with no heat entering.
questions.hint: Use Tf = Ti (Vi/Vf)^(gamma - 1) for adiabatic expansion.

Divided pressure by the volume change
Doubled the volume change before multiplying

questions.explanation: At constant pressure the work done by the gas is P delta V. With pressure 167 kPa and volume increase 6.8 L, and using one kPa litre equal to one joule, the work is 1136 J. A rigid constant-volume step would instead do zero work, but this process has a moving piston.

Added the absorbed and rejected heat instead of subtracting
Reported the absorbed heat as the useful work

questions.explanation: Because the device returns to its starting state each cycle, the change in internal energy over a full cycle is zero, so the net work output equals the net heat input Qh minus Qc. That gives 352 J per cycle; the rejected heat is not available as work.
